description: Terravect is a solo team focused on using software, AI, and data science to solve real-world problems with NASA data. I have experience building full-stack applications, working with machine learning, and developing data-driven tools. My goal is to create an innovative, scientifically grounded solution with a strong emphasis on functionality, accuracy, and real-world impact.
summary:
Environmental data can reveal how our planet is changing, but understanding those changes requires more than plotting a graph. 

TrendLens is an interactive, open-source scientific investigation platform that makes NASA Earth science data more accessible to students, educators, and citizen scientists.

Built for NASA's 'Be An Earth System Trend Detective!' challenge, TrendLens transforms complex temperature datasets into guided, reproducible investigations. Its primary demonstration analyzes 24 complete years (2002–2025) of NASA Giovanni MERRA-2 temperature data for a region near Abu Dhabi. Users can visualize historical patterns, calculate rates of change, examine uncertainty, and download the original evidence and methodology. A second investigation compares NASA POWER temperature data for Abu Dhabi and Oslo over consistent time periods.

What distinguishes TrendLens is its emphasis on scientific transparency. Instead of presenting every apparent trend as a proven conclusion, it explains statistical limitations, distinguishes descriptive trends from validated significance, and preserves data provenance.

Our goal is to make environmental analysis more understandable, reproducible, and scientifically responsible.
details:
TrendLens is an open-source Earth science investigation platform developed by Team Terravect for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It transforms NASA environmental datasets into accessible, interactive, and reproducible scientific investigations.

While NASA provides powerful tools for accessing Earth observation data, interpreting long-term environmental trends can still require specialized knowledge in data processing and statistics. TrendLens helps bridge this gap for students, educators, and citizen scientists.

Users can explore environmental temperature records, investigate historical patterns, compare geographical locations, and examine the evidence behind calculated trends.

Our primary investigation uses NASA Giovanni to analyze MERRA-2 monthly air-temperature data for a region near Abu Dhabi. From 24 complete years of measurements (2002–2025), TrendLens estimates a descriptive warming trend of approximately +0.356°C per decade.

A second investigation uses NASA POWER data to compare Abu Dhabi and Oslo across 25 shared years (2001–2025).

The platform provides interactive visualizations, annual temperature calculations, trend estimates, uncertainty information, data-coverage checks, and downloadable scientific investigation reports.

TrendLens goes beyond displaying environmental graphs by creating a guided, evidence-first investigation experience.

Its distinguishing capabilities include:

  • Scientific transparency: Clearly separates observed patterns and descriptive estimates from conclusions that require further statistical validation.
  • Reproducibility: Preserves original NASA data, provenance, processing methods, and SHA-256 checksums.
  • Consistent comparisons: Aligns time periods across locations and provides both absolute-temperature and relative-change visualizations.
  • Accessibility: Explains scientific findings in understandable language without requiring users to write code.

Rather than creating another climate model, TrendLens makes existing NASA scientific information easier to investigate critically.

TrendLens uses genuine NASA data, excludes incomplete years from annual analyses, performs documented unit conversions, and retains the source measurements.

Our trend estimates use ordinary least-squares regression. Because temporal autocorrelation has not been adequately accounted for, we do not claim validated statistical significance, causal attribution, or definitive climate-change detection.

These limitations are explicitly presented to users rather than hidden.

TrendLens was developed using Python, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly, and NASA data services. It is hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, with publicly available source code on GitHub under the MIT license.

Our objective is to make NASA Earth science data more accessible, understandable, and reproducible. TrendLens could support classroom investigations, citizen science, and exploratory environmental research by helping users evaluate evidence rather than simply interpret isolated graphs.

Live application: https://terravect-trendlens.streamlit.app/

Source code: https://github.com/laithmunir9/terravect-trendlens
